claims.text: The coupled tribo-corrosion response is governed by formation of a mechanically mixed layer.
The mechanically mixed layer enhances corrosion protection.
The mechanically mixed layer increases wear by introducing corrosive species into the wear process.
The alloy is tested in the as-cast state.
The proposed tribo-corrosion test uses a normal load of 50 N.
The proposed tribo-corrosion test uses a sliding speed of 0.1 m/s.
The proposed tribo-corrosion test uses a potential of -0.5 V versus Ag/AgCl.
The proposed environment is 3.5% NaCl at 25 °C.
The mechanically mixed layer acts as a barrier that reduces corrosion current density.
Corrosive species incorporated into the wear process increase the wear rate.
The corrosion rate will decrease by 20% relative to the baseline.
The wear rate will increase by 15% relative to the baseline.
Total degradation will increase by 5% relative to the baseline.
The baseline is the high-entropy alloy subjected to corrosion only.
The prediction should hold for FeCoCrNiMn alloys with grain sizes of 10–50 μm.
The prediction may fail for alloys with substantially different compositions or microstructures.
The exact mechanism of mechanically mixed layer formation and its effect on coupled wear-corrosion response is not well understood.
The mechanism may vary with alloy composition and testing conditions.
The proposed falsification experiment varies normal load and corrosion potential while measuring corrosion current density, wear rate, and mechanically mixed layer thickness.
The hypothesis is falsified if corrosion rate rises by more than 10% and wear rate falls by more than 10% relative to the baseline.

contradictions.description: A corrosion-only baseline has no wear component, so a 15% relative increase in wear rate cannot be defined against that baseline.
The falsification rule requires a relative decrease in wear rate, but the specified corrosion-only baseline does not provide a baseline wear rate.

A 5% increase in total degradation is not coherently determined from a 20% corrosion decrease and 15% wear increase without defining component magnitudes and a common total-degradation metric; this is especially problematic because the baseline contains no wear.
